title: Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging

concept.text: This proposed innovation would restore both reproductive and hormonal ovarian function after natural menopause: the person's ovaries would again support the maturation of competent oocytes and produce cyclic endogenous sex hormones. The target is sustained function that can support conception and live birth, rather than an isolated increase in a hormone measurement. The ovary's paired roles as a source of oocytes and sex hormones make both functions central to the concept.

Scope synthesis: success would make the natural menopausal transition functionally reversible for successfully treated people. Improving fertility during perimenopause, treating primary ovarian insufficiency, and restoring function after established natural menopause are distinct achievements. Improvements in the first two settings could inform this innovation but would not, by themselves, demonstrate the third.

significance.text: The female reproductive system is among the first systems to show age-related functional decline, and people can live for decades after menopause. Restoring its reproductive and endocrine functions would therefore address a substantial interval of life. The supplied evidence supports this early-aging framing, but does not establish the stronger claim that the ovary is the first major organ system to fail.

Conditional impact synthesis: if sustained reversal were achieved, direct consequences would include renewed ovarian cycles, endogenous cyclic estrogen and progesterone production, and a chance of conception using oocytes from the person's own ovary without a donor oocyte. Oocyte freezing preserves younger oocytes, ovarian tissue cryopreservation preserves tissue, and hormone replacement supplies hormonal signals. Restoring an aged ovary's combined functions would extend beyond each of those capabilities.

Impact limits: restored ovarian function would not by itself establish prevention of cardiovascular disease, fractures, or dementia, nor would it establish reversal of aging elsewhere in the body. Those possible downstream benefits would require separate clinical evidence. Restored fertility would also not establish that pregnancy at every later age is safe. Cancer risk would require explicit assessment and follow-up; no finite study could guarantee its absence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is sustained restoration of an ovarian environment that supports competent oocytes and cyclic hormone secretion after natural menopause. The biological obstacles include depletion of a finite primordial follicle pool, DNA damage and chromosomal abnormalities, and an increasingly fibrotic and inflammatory ovarian environment. These are related barriers, but they are not interchangeable: making the surrounding tissue more supportive does not establish that an exhausted follicle reserve has been replenished or that age-related oocyte abnormalities have been corrected.

The supplied animal findings show that modifying ovarian tissue can improve some measures of function. They leave unresolved whether such interventions can supply enough developmentally competent oocytes after established menopause. Reduced DNA-damage markers in granulosa cells, which support the oocyte, cannot be treated as proof that oocyte chromosome abnormalities have been repaired. Similarly, more observed follicles or higher antimüllerian hormone (AMH) does not establish creation of a new follicle reserve.

Engineering synthesis: a practical treatment would need a reproducible intervention, delivery method, dose, and patient-selection strategy that produce durable endocrine and reproductive benefits with acceptable risks. It would also need to establish what biological resource sustains the response—remaining follicles, replenished follicles, or another demonstrated mechanism. Activation of residual follicles could contribute to a successful treatment, but a short-lived response would not establish sustained reversal.

current_state.text: Amargant, Magalhaes, Pritchard, Duncan, and colleagues reported that six weeks of systemic pirfenidone reduced age-associated ovarian fibrosis in mice and improved follicle counts, corpora lutea counts, AMH levels, and estrous cyclicity. The study appeared online on 16 September 2024 and in GeroScience 2025;47:3475–3495, DOI 10.1007/s11357-024-01322-w. These are mouse findings and do not establish human reproductive efficacy. The supplied review's assessment rests on a subscription preview and abstract-level outcomes. A separately supplied PDF contained supplemental figures rather than the main paper, had extraction warnings, and its graphics were not visually inspected, so it did not provide independent confirmation.

Yan, Tu, Wang, and colleagues transplanted human embryonic-stem-cell-derived mesenchymal-stromal-cell-like M cells into naturally aging cynomolgus ovaries. Their Cell Discovery study, published 5 November 2024 as 10:111, DOI 10.1038/s41421-024-00726-4, included seven treated and three control monkeys aged 18–23 years, selected for perimenopause. The authors reported reduced fibrosis and granulosa-cell DNA-damage markers, increased sex-hormone secretion, and one natural conception resulting in a healthy full-term offspring, with offspring health reported through three years. This is a nonhuman-primate proof of principle during perimenopause, rather than reversal of established menopause in humans.

The primate findings have important limits beyond species and menopausal stage. One offspring does not establish a reliable reproductive success rate. Histology used one ovary per group at each sampled interval, and some comparisons were based on sections rather than independent animals; those comparisons therefore should not be interpreted as broad animal-level replication. The supplied review had full article text available, but did not visually inspect the figures, so its interpretation relies on explicit text and methods.

Seyihoglu, Gucuk, and Can reviewed human cellular therapies for primary ovarian insufficiency and poor ovarian reserve in Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics 2025;42:2837–2857, DOI 10.1007/s10815-025-03599-y. The accessible abstract reports that 77.8% of studies lacked controls and that 60 of 522 treated patients became pregnant, compared with 13 of 172 controls. The counts correspond to approximately 11.5% and 7.6%; the abstract instead prints 11.7% for the treated group. This numerical inconsistency remains unresolved. These heterogeneous pooled pregnancy counts do not establish comparative treatment efficacy, live-birth benefit, or reversal of natural menopause. Access in the supplied review was partial, limiting assessment of individual studies and their methods.

The research also cited a review attributed to Fertility and Sterility 2026;125:387–398 and attributed to it a conclusion that routine intraovarian anti-aging interventions were premature. No source text was captured for that citation, so the supplied review could verify neither its bibliographic identity nor its attributed conclusion. It cannot serve as evidence for that conclusion here, and no DOI should be inferred from its article identifier. This access limitation does not establish that the article or its reported conclusion is false.

Evidence-bound synthesis: the sources assessed in the supplied review do not demonstrate controlled, sustained restoration of fertile ovarian function after natural menopause in humans. They document animal improvements and limited human cellular-therapy outcomes in other ovarian conditions. Because the supplied freshness record is empty, they do not establish the universal claim that no such human treatment existed as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established consensus standard: enroll people with confirmed natural menopause who did not have ovarian tissue cryopreserved, and show sustained cyclic endogenous hormone production together with production of euploid oocytes capable of supporting healthy pregnancies and live births. Euploidy—an appropriate chromosome complement—would be one endpoint, not a substitute for evidence of embryo development, pregnancy, and offspring outcomes. The study should distinguish endogenous ovarian function from administered hormonal signals.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained endogenous cycles and euploid oocytes support healthy live births

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and causal tests: use appropriate comparison groups, prespecified follow-up duration, repeated-cycle endpoints, and transparent reporting of all enrolled participants. Establish whether benefits persist beyond transient stimulation of a few residual follicles. Residual-follicle activation need not disqualify an otherwise durable result, but a single ovulation, a rise in AMH, reduced mouse fibrosis, or one primate birth would not meet the combined human endocrine and reproductive goal.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled repeated-cycle follow-up establishes durable endocrine and reproductive benefits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and safety boundaries: independently reproduce the result using a defined intervention and report its success rate across relevant ages, time since menopause, and baseline ovarian characteristics. Prespecify maternal and offspring follow-up, including assessment of cancer risk and other intervention-related harms. Finite trials could establish benefit, durability, and observed safety within studied populations and follow-up periods; they could not establish universal effectiveness, indefinite restoration, or zero lifetime risk.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reports stratified success rates and observed safety limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell, shares the goal of obtaining competent oocytes when the existing supply is inadequate. Its stated target is gamete manufacture; OBG-05 requires restoration of ovarian reproductive and cyclic endocrine function after natural menopause. Producing an oocyte outside the body would not by itself rejuvenate the ovary. An eventual combination of approaches is conceivable, but it is not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Roster-based comparison: OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis, and OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, overlap with OBG-05 in reproductive health and preservation of fertility. Their targets remain distinct: endometriosis, cancer interception, and ovarian reproductive aging. Cancer-risk evaluation is a safety requirement for ovarian restoration, rather than evidence that OBG-05 also achieves OBG-09.

Roster-based comparison: OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, addresses the capacity to carry a pregnancy. OBG-05 addresses ovarian oocytes and hormones. These could be complementary capabilities, but restoring ovarian function would not establish that a manufactured uterus can support gestation, and manufacturing a uterus would not restore an aged ovarian reserve.

Roster-based comparison: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock; OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap; OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency; OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease; and OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, concern later reproductive stages or support of an existing pregnancy or developing fetus. They could affect outcomes following conception, but none of their supplied titles describes restoration of postmenopausal ovarian function. These distinctions are based on roster titles, rather than detailed definitions or evidence supplied for those concepts.

unresolved_issues: Whether any human intervention had achieved sustained fertile ovarian restoration after natural menopause by 1 November 2026 remains unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
Whether environmental treatment can overcome a severely depleted follicle reserve or age-related oocyte chromosome abnormalities remains unresolved.

The human cellular-therapy review's reported 11.7% pregnancy rate conflicts with its count of 60 pregnancies among 522 treated patients; the supplied material does not resolve which element is erroneous.
The identity and attributed conclusion of the cited 2026 Fertility and Sterility review remain unverified because no source text was captured.
The durability, reproducibility, human efficacy, maternal safety, offspring outcomes, and cancer risks of a successful postmenopausal restoration treatment remain to be established.
Appropriate treatment-specific duration thresholds and patient-selection boundaries require justification; the proposed completion criteria are not established consensus standards.

brief.title: Restored fertility and hormone cycles after menopause
possible: After natural menopause, people could again have a chance of conceiving with eggs from their own ovaries. Their ovaries would also resume making estrogen and progesterone in sustained cycles.
why: People can live for decades after menopause. Restoring ovarian function would reopen reproductive choices during that part of life and restore the body's own cyclic hormone production, going beyond what hormone replacement or previously frozen eggs provide.

sources.who: Farners Amargant, Carol Magalhaes, Michele T. Pritchard, Francesca E. Duncan
sources.showed: Pirfenidone, a drug that reduces tissue scarring, reduced scarring in aging mouse ovaries. Treated mice had more follicles, the structures containing eggs, and more regular reproductive cycles.
sources.quote: Pirfenidone mitigated the age-dependent increase in ovarian fibrosis without impacting overall health parameters.
sources.cited_for: Changing the tissue surrounding eggs can improve ovarian function in aging mice.
sources.not_established: The mouse results do not establish restored human fertility after natural menopause.

sources.who: Long Yan, Wan Tu, Hongmei Wang and colleagues
sources.showed: Cells grown from human embryonic stem cells reduced ovarian scarring and increased sex-hormone secretion in monkeys approaching menopause. A treated monkey gave birth to a healthy offspring.
sources.quote: Encouragingly, a healthy baby monkey was born after M-cell transplantation.
sources.cited_for: Cell treatment improved ovarian function and supported a live birth in an aging primate.
sources.not_established: A single birth in a small study before menopause does not establish reliable fertility restoration after human menopause.

sources.who: Burakhan Seyihoglu, Sude Gucuk and Alp Can
sources.showed: Their review found pregnancies after cell treatments for ovaries that stopped working early or had few eggs remaining. Most studies lacked comparison groups, limiting conclusions about treatment effects.
sources.quote: Pregnancy outcomes were reported in 59.2% of studies with control groups.
sources.cited_for: Human cell treatments have been studied in ovarian conditions distinct from natural menopause.
sources.not_established: The pooled results do not establish treatment efficacy, improved live-birth outcomes or reversal of natural menopause.

sources.showed: This is a review of anti-aging interventions delivered into the ovaries.
sources.cited_for: It concerns proposed treatments for ovarian aging.
sources.not_established: A review does not itself demonstrate restored fertility and hormone cycles after natural menopause.

shown: Yan and colleagues reached the clearest reproductive result: one healthy offspring after cell treatment in monkeys approaching menopause. Mouse experiments also improved ovarian function. These results do not yet demonstrate sustained restoration of fertility and hormone cycles after established natural menopause in humans.
missing: Human trials have yet to demonstrate lasting ovarian hormone cycles and healthy live births after confirmed natural menopause.
No treatment has shown that it can sustain enough eggs capable of healthy development after menopause.
A reproducible treatment needs to establish lasting benefits and acceptable risks for treated people and their offspring.

milestones.label: Sustained ovarian cycles and healthy live births after menopause
milestones.explanation: People with confirmed natural menopause and no frozen ovarian tissue would need sustained self-produced hormone cycles and eggs with normal chromosome sets supporting healthy live births. This would demonstrate both ovarian functions.

milestones.label: Controlled studies establish lasting hormone and reproductive benefits
milestones.explanation: Studies with comparison groups, a predefined follow-up period and results for all participants would need to show benefits across repeated cycles. This would distinguish durable restoration from briefly stimulating a few remaining eggs.

milestones.label: Independent studies establish success rates and observed safety
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would need to reproduce success across ages, time since menopause and starting ovarian condition, while tracking maternal, offspring and cancer risks. This would establish who benefits and the observed safety limits.

uncertain: Can improving ovarian tissue overcome a severely depleted egg supply and age-related chromosome abnormalities in eggs?
How long must restored function last, and which patients should qualify? These proposed milestones are not agreed clinical standards.
Restored ovarian function would not establish that later-age pregnancy is safe or that aging elsewhere in the body has reversed.

page.title: Restoration of ovarian function after natural menopause
page.definition: After natural menopause, ovaries would again release oocytes (egg cells), produce recurring endogenous estradiol and progesterone cycles, and support live birth using eggs matured after treatment. Natural menopause requires 12 consecutive months without menstruation, without another physiological or pathological cause or a clinical intervention explaining its absence.

goal.need: In 2021, women aged 50 and over constituted 26% of all women and girls globally, compared with 22% in 2011. Menopause ends ovarian egg release and lowers circulating oestrogen. The age and life-expectancy estimates show the interval that ovarian restoration would address. Restoration targets the loss of both fertility and endogenous ovarian hormone secretion.

completion.title: A treatment restores ovarian hormone cycles and own-oocyte live birth after natural menopause.
completion.criterion: A controlled human study demonstrates treatment-attributable restoration of recurrent ovulation and endogenous estradiol–progesterone cycles after confirmed natural menopause, together with live birth from oocytes matured in the treated ovaries after treatment. Menopause must meet the 12-month definition. Donor eggs, previously stored eggs or embryos, and previously cryopreserved ovarian tissue do not qualify. Administered sex hormones cannot constitute endocrine recovery. Follow-up must be prespecified; no consensus minimum duration or success rate was identified.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external body identified a combined postmenopausal reproductive-and-endocrine completion test.
completion.basis: Searched WHO definitions, ASRM guidance and ICMART terminology, the Endocrine Society statement, ARPA-H ovarian-health targets, NAM prize projects and ovarian-restoration protocols. No combined completion test or durability threshold was found. This fallback combines the published fertility and endocrine goals and requires causal evidence beyond the uncontrolled human birth report.

milestones.title: A cell-based ovarian treatment demonstrates safety and efficacy in a relevant preclinical model.
milestones.criterion: For the cell-based route, demonstrate preclinical safety and efficacy in models matched to the proposed clinical condition and tissue physiology. ISSCR specifies no ovarian-specific numerical bar. A paper published on 5 November 2024 reported 1 full-term birth in 7 treated cynomolgus monkeys and none in 3 controls; ages were 18–23 years and all were perimenopausal. This does not establish reversal after menopause. Mouse pirfenidone work reported improved cyclicity after 6 weeks; group sizes were unavailable in the accessible abstract.
milestones.set_by: International Society for Stem Cell Research, Guidelines, recommendations 3.3.1.2 and 3.3.3.1; these apply to stem-cell-based interventions.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early phase human studies should be preceded by a rigorous demonstration of safety and efficacy in preclinical studies.

milestones.title: Menstruation returns and FSH falls within 3 months after treatment of natural menopause.
milestones.criterion: The menopausal pilot protocol requires menstrual-cycle restoration and reduced follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) during 3 months of follow-up. Eligibility: age 45–55 years, at least 12 months without menstruation or hormone replacement, and FSH >30 IU/L. No required FSH decrease or responder fraction was specified. The paper published on 10 June 2020 reported this response in 13/30 participants without controls. A 2025 cellular-therapy review concerned premature ovarian insufficiency and poor reserve (27 studies; 694 patients); it does not establish this natural-menopause endpoint.
milestones.set_by: Genesis Athens Clinic, menopausal pilot protocol approved by the Centre for Human Reproduction Ethics Board, as published in J Clin Med (2020).
milestones.threshold_quote: Regarding the POI and menopausal groups, the primary outcome measures entailed restoration of menstrual cycle as well as FSH levels.

milestones.title: A treated postmenopausal participant has luteal serum progesterone above 3 ng/mL, indicating ovulation.
milestones.criterion: Measure serum progesterone approximately 1 week before expected menstruation; a value >3 ng/mL provides presumptive evidence of recent ovulation. For endogenous recovery, administered progesterone must not explain the result. This single-cycle diagnostic criterion does not establish fertile luteal function or durability. The cited menopausal pilot measured FSH, LH, estradiol and AMH, but not progesterone, so it does not document this assay-defined endpoint.
milestones.set_by: American Society for Reproductive Medicine Practice Committee, Fertility evaluation of infertile women (2026); an ovulation criterion, not a menopause-reversal standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: A progesterone concentration >3 ng/mL provides presumptive and sufficient evidence of recent ovulation

milestones.title: A treated postmenopausal participant has a live birth from an oocyte matured after treatment.
milestones.criterion: An oocyte matured after treatment supports a birth after 22 completed weeks of gestation with breathing or another sign of life; birth weight ≥500 g may substitute when gestational age is unknown. Previously stored or donor reproductive material is excluded by this entry’s scope. The 2020 uncontrolled menopausal pilot reported 1 natural conception and term live birth among 30 treated participants. That observation does not establish treatment efficacy or recurring endogenous hormone cycles.
milestones.set_by: ICMART and endorsing fertility societies, The International Glossary on Infertility and Fertility Care, 2025, published in 2026; the live-birth definition appears in a table. Postmenopausal status and oocyte origin delimit this entry.

not_found: No controlled study establishing both recurring endogenous ovarian cycles and own-oocyte live birth after natural menopause was identified.
Direct ClinicalTrials.gov endpoint text for NCT03916978 could not be retrieved.
The accessible mouse-paper preview did not provide experimental group sizes.
The supplied Fertility and Sterility publisher page could not be opened; the review’s full text was unavailable.

results.finding: Pirfenidone-treated mice showed improved estrous cyclicity after 6 weeks; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The treatment was a systemic drug, not a cell-based ovarian treatment. The abstract does not establish a model of natural menopause or report group sizes.
results.quote: Ovarian function was improved in Pirfenidone-treated mice as evidenced by increased follicle and corpora lutea number, AMH levels, and improved estrous cyclicity.

results.finding: Among 7 treated perimenopausal cynomolgus monkeys, 1 delivered a full-term baby; none of 3 controls conceived.
results.detail: The study reported no acute inflammation or malignant disease during follow-up. The monkeys were perimenopausal, so the model did not match the postmenopausal condition.
results.quote: The pregnant monkey finally delivered a healthy full-term baby.

results.finding: In 18-month-old mice, LRP1-high cell treatment shortened estrous cycles (P < 0.0001); group size not stated in the text.
results.detail: The aged mice had impaired ovarian function but were not shown to model natural postmenopause. Treated mice had implanted embryos, but live births were not reported. The text describes preliminary safety assessments without establishing comprehensive safety.
